t.6.45.1: Hearing of the slaying of Akampana, the lord of the rākṣasas was enraged indeed, and, his face somewhat downcast, he looked toward those ministers of his.
t.6.45.2: But he, having reflected for a moment and deliberated with his ministers, went around the city of Laṅkā to inspect all the troop posts.
t.6.45.3: He beheld the city of Laṅkā, guarded by hosts of Rākṣasas, encircled by many troops, and garlanded with banners and flags.
t.6.45.4: Seeing the city besieged, Rāvaṇa, lord of the rākṣasas, enraged, spoke at that time to Prahasta, who was skilled in war.
t.6.45.6: Either I, or Kumbhakarṇa, or you, the commander of my army, or Indrajit, or Nikumbha could bear a burden such as this.
t.6.45.5: For this city, besieged and suddenly hard pressed, I see no deliverance other than battle, O you who are skilled in warfare.
t.6.45.7: Therefore you, quickly taking an army from here and keeping it well in hand, march out for victory to where all the forest-dwellers are.
t.6.45.8: Surely, at your very going forth, the fickle army of monkeys will flee upon hearing the roar of the roaring lords of the Rākṣasas.
t.6.45.9: For the monkeys are fickle, undisciplined and unsteady of mind; they will not endure your roar, just as elephants cannot endure the roar of a lion.
t.6.45.10: And when that army of yours has fled, Rāma together with Saumitri, helpless and without support, will fall into the power of Prahasta.
t.6.45.11: Better is a calamity whose outcome is still in doubt; here it has not yet been made certain. Whether it runs against us or in our favour, tell us whatever you consider beneficial for us.
t.6.45.12: Thus addressed by Rāvaṇa, Prahasta, the commander of the army, spoke these words to the lord of the Rākṣasas, as Uśanas once spoke to the lord of the Asuras.
t.6.45.13: O king, we have already taken counsel together with skilled ministers, and a debate also took place among us as we examined the matter with one another.
t.6.45.14: I had determined that welfare lay in the giving back of Sītā, but in not giving her back there would be war; this is just how we had seen it.
t.6.45.15: I, who have constantly been honored by you with gifts and marks of respect and with kind words of many kinds, what would I not do to please you when the time has come?
t.6.45.16: For my life is not something I must guard, nor my sons, wives or wealth. Behold me, eager to offer up my life as an oblation in battle for your sake.
t.6.45.17: Having spoken thus to his master Rāvaṇa, the commander of the army said, "Quickly assemble for me a great force of rākṣasas."
t.6.45.18: Today let the birds be sated with the flesh of the forest-dwellers, slain on the field of battle by the force of my thunderbolt-like arrows.
t.6.45.19: Thus addressed by Prahasta, those commanders of the army, acting with haste, roused the army to readiness in that abode of the rākṣasas.
t.6.45.20: In a moment that Laṅkā became thronged with those Rākṣasa heroes bearing sharp weapons of many kinds, as though crowded with elephants.
t.6.45.21: As they gratified the sacrificial fire and paid homage to the brāhmaṇas, a fragrant breeze blew, carrying the scent of clarified butter.
t.6.45.23: Armed with bows and clad in armour, the rākṣasas leapt up swiftly and, after looking toward King Rāvaṇa, surrounded Prahasta.
t.6.45.24: Then, having taken leave of the king and having struck a terrifying kettledrum, Prahasta mounted his divine chariot, which had been made ready and equipped for battle.
t.6.45.22: Then the delighted Rākṣasas took up garlands of various forms, consecrated with mantras, and put on their battle gear.
t.6.45.25: A chariot yoked with horses of great speed, properly furnished with a skilled charioteer, thundering like a great rain-cloud, and shining brilliantly like the very moon and sun.
t.6.45.26: He mounted the chariot, unassailable with its serpent banner, with a fine protective fender and excellent fittings, adorned with a network of gold, and seeming almost to laugh with its splendour.
t.6.45.27: Then, mounting that chariot, he who had been entrusted with Rāvaṇa's command swiftly went forth from Laṅkā, surrounded by a great army.
t.6.45.28: Then, as the commander of the army set forth, the thunderous sound of kettledrums, like the roaring of a rain-cloud, was heard, and the blare of conches as well.
t.6.45.29: Roaring terrible cries, the rākṣasas went on ahead, fearsome in form and huge of body, as the vanguard of Prahasta.
t.6.45.30: He sallied forth from the eastern gate, surrounded by a great and most dreadful army drawn up in battle array, resembling a herd of elephants.
t.6.45.31: Surrounded by that army, which was like the flood of the ocean, Prahasta, enraged and resembling Kāla, the Ender, swiftly marched forth.
t.6.45.32: At the clamour of his setting forth, and of the roaring rākṣasas, all creatures in Laṅkā cried out with distorted voices.
t.6.45.34: Fearsome jackals howled, vomiting flames of fire.
t.6.45.33: Birds that feed on flesh and blood rose into the cloudless sky and wheeled in inauspicious counterclockwise circles over the chariot.
t.6.45.35: A meteor fell from the sky, and a harsh wind blew; the planets, enraged against one another, did not shine.
t.6.45.36: They rained blood upon him and drenched those who marched before him, and on the top of his banner a vulture settled, facing south.
t.6.45.37: And as he plunged into the battle, the goad fell again and again from the hand of his charioteer, the sūta who drove his horses.
t.6.45.38: The splendour of his setting-out, radiant and very hard to attain, vanished in a moment, and all his horses stumbled.
t.6.45.39: But as Prahasta, renowned for his strength and valor, came marching out, the army of monkeys, bearing weapons of many kinds, advanced against him in battle.
t.6.45.40: Then there arose a most tumultuous uproar from the monkeys as they tore up trees and seized heavy rocks.
t.6.45.41: Both armies were exultant, and a mighty roar was heard from the hosts of rākṣasas and the forest-dwellers, impetuous and powerful, each eager to slay the other and challenging one another.
t.6.45.42: Then the evil-minded Prahasta set out for victory against the army of the king of the monkeys, and he entered that host of ever-mounting force as a moth bent on death enters a fire.
